# Meanwhile

It is 3:14 a.m., and somewhere a woman is standing barefoot in her kitchen, drinking orange juice straight from the carton because the glasses are all dirty and she has decided, tonight, that this is who she is now. The refrigerator light makes a yellow rectangle on the tile. She watches dust drift through it like slow snow. In eleven hours she will apologize to no one for anything.

Meanwhile, four thousand miles away, a man is walking his dog along a canal at dusk, and the dog stops to stare at a moored boat as if it has never seen one before, though it sees this same boat every day. The man waits. He is learning, slowly, from the dog, how to be interested in ordinary things again. His daughter used to point at pigeons and say their names — *bird, bird, bird* — as if each one deserved its own introduction. She is grown now. He still introduces himself to evenings sometimes, quietly, just to practice.

Meanwhile, in a hospital room lit only by monitors, a nurse is doing a crossword puzzle at 3:15 a.m. She is stuck on a seven-letter word for "the space between." She thinks: *interval*. No. *Liminal*. Too many letters, or too few, she can't remember. Her grandmother used to say that the hour before dawn belonged to no one, that you could hear the world thinking. The nurse believes this completely and has built her entire life around it. Down the hall, her patient sleeps with his mouth open, breathing in the particular way of people who are going to be okay.

Meanwhile, a teenager in a basement bedroom is teaching herself to play guitar from videos, and her fingers hurt so much she wants to cry, and she keeps playing anyway because there is a chord — just one, F minor, or maybe it's B flat, she loses track — that sounds exactly the way rain on a school window feels. She doesn't have words for that yet. She has the chord instead. Words will come later, and they will be worse, and then better, and then worse again, which is the whole shape of a life.

Meanwhile, on a container ship in the middle of the Pacific, the second officer stands his watch under more stars than seem legally permitted. The sea is black velvet with a slow green shimmer where the bow cuts it. He thinks about his wife asleep in their apartment above the bakery, how the whole building must smell like tomorrow's bread by now. He calculates distances out of habit. He does not calculate the distance between missing someone and being glad to be alone; some measurements ruin the thing they measure.

Meanwhile, an old woman in a wheelchair by a nursing home window is watching a squirrel bury something in the courtyard and forget where. She laughs. The aide asks what's funny, and she says, "He'll find it or he won't," as if this explained everything, which it does.

Meanwhile, in a city apartment, two people who met nine days ago are lying awake on opposite sides of a bed, both pretending to sleep, both composing sentences they will not say. Between them, the mattress holds its breath. One of them is counting ceiling cracks. The other is remembering, inexplicably, a swimming lesson from age six, the shock of cold water, the enormous hands that caught her. She decides that love is probably like that: terrifying mostly because someone might catch you.

Meanwhile, a baker turns on his ovens. Meanwhile, a fisherman curses the engine that won't start. Meanwhile, a boy in a refugee camp teaches another boy a card game using a deck missing the sevens, and they agree without discussion that sevens are not needed for happiness. Meanwhile, a poet crumples paper. Meanwhile, the paper uncrumples slightly in the wastebasket overnight, forgiving her.

And meanwhile — this is the part nobody tells you — all of it is happening at once. Not sequentially, not in any order that respects importance. The orange juice and the crossword and the chord that hurts to play. The stars over the ship and the squirrel's forgotten acorn and the hands that catch. There is no narrator deciding whose moment matters most. There is only the great simultaneous hum of it, billions of small scenes lit from within, overlapping like radio stations bleeding across frequencies at the edge of reception.

If you could hear it all at once — really hear it — it would sound like static, and if you listened long enough, the static would resolve into something almost like a voice, and if you leaned closer it would say something simple and unbearable, something like:

*You are one of these. You are the kitchen light and the canal and the seven-letter word. Right now, while you read this, someone is falling asleep to your memory, someone is laughing at nothing in a hallway, someone is choosing to keep going for reasons they couldn't list under oath. The world is not waiting for you to begin. It began. It is mid-sentence everywhere.*

At 3:17 a.m., the woman rinses the juice carton and puts it in the recycling, because even rebels have standards. The dog finally moves on from the boat. The nurse writes *liminal* in the margin, just to look at it. The girl plays the chord one more time, and gets it clean, and sits very still afterward, holding the guitar like a small animal that trusts her.

The old woman watches the squirrel leave. The baker smells cinnamon. The ship moves north.

Nothing happens next. That is, everything does — but gently, in parallel, in the dark, the way grass grows: invisibly, everywhere, all at once, indifferent and devoted, until morning comes and finds the whole world changed by a millimeter and calls it a day.

---

*(Word count: ~1,000)*
